module

public import Mathlib.NumberTheory.ArithmeticFunction.Misc

@[expose] public section

/-!
# Amicable numbers

Two natural numbers $a$ and $b$ are amicable if $\sigma(a) = \sigma(b) = a + b$,
where $\sigma$ is the sum-of-divisors function.
-/

open scoped ArithmeticFunction.sigma

/--
We say that $a,b\in \mathbb{N}$ are an amicable pair if $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$.
-/
@[mk_iff]
structure IsAmicable (a b : ℕ) : Prop where
  left : σ 1 a = a + b
  right : σ 1 b = a + b

findings.description: The structure at lines 35–37 requires only the two sigma equalities, omitting distinctness. It describes aliquot periods dividing two, whereas an amicable pair has two distinct members. In scratch Lean I proved `IsAmicable n n ↔ n = 0 ∨ Nat.Perfect n`, and verified `IsAmicable 0 0`, `IsAmicable 6 6`, and `IsAmicable 28 28`. Thus it admits both Mathlib's zero default and every perfect-number diagonal. The docstrings repeat the incomplete characterization rather than stating the standard notion.
findings.source_evidence: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amicable_numbers, defines amicable numbers as “two different natural numbers” and distinguishes aliquot period two from the period-one case of perfect numbers. Pomerance, On amicable numbers (2015), §1, https://math.dartmouth.edu/~carlp/amicablesv3.pdf, explicitly requires “Two different positive integers a, b”. Mathlib's ArithmeticFunction maps zero to zero, and Nat.Perfect explicitly requires positivity.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a field `ne : a ≠ b` to `IsAmicable` and correct both docstrings. Separate positivity fields are unnecessary: the sigma equalities together with `a ≠ b` imply `0 < a ∧ 0 < b`. I proved that this corrected predicate is equivalent to distinct positive integers whose proper-divisor sums equal each other. If the broader period-dividing-two relation is also wanted, keep it separate from the standard amicable predicate.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/830.lean, the filter `a ≤ b ∧ IsAmicable a b` counts every positive perfect number n ≤ x as an amicable pair `(n,n)`. I proved `Erdos830.A 6 = 1` and `Erdos830.A 28 = 2`; the genuine amicable-pair count is zero at both cutoffs. More generally, the implemented count equals the genuine pair count plus the perfect-number count, as verified by a finite-set decomposition in scratch Lean.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/830 asks for the count of amicable pairs with `1 ≤ a ≤ b ≤ x` and links to Wikipedia's distinct-member definition. Its abbreviated sigma characterization omits distinctness, but the underlying Erdős paper, On amicable numbers (1955), p. 110, https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1955-03.pdf, explicitly enumerates the pairs with `a_i < b_i`. Wikipedia and the paper identify `(220,284)` as the smallest pair.
findings.suggested_fix: Fix `IsAmicable` globally by requiring distinctness. Alternatively, while retaining the broader predicate, change the filter to `a < b ∧ IsAmicable a b`. The positive intervals and natural floor otherwise handle the counting domain correctly.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/830.lean, `{(a,b) | IsAmicable a b}.Infinite` includes all perfect-number diagonals. I proved that its right-hand side is equivalent to the disjunction “infinitely many genuine amicable pairs OR infinitely many perfect numbers”. This allows a positive answer solely through the separate perfect-number infinitude problem, instead of requiring infinitely many distinct-member amicable pairs. The extra `(0,0)` and the use of ordered pairs do not themselves affect infinitude; the potentially infinite diagonal family does.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/830 poses infinitude of amicable pairs and links to https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amicable_numbers, which explicitly requires different members. Erdős's original 1955 paper, pp. 108–110, https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1955-03.pdf, poses this infinitude problem and enumerates pairs with `a_i < b_i`. Pomerance's 2015 introduction also states the infinitude question after explicitly requiring different positive integers.
findings.suggested_fix: Fix the shared predicate, or use `answer(sorry) ↔ {p : ℕ × ℕ | p.1 ≠ p.2 ∧ IsAmicable p.1 p.2}.Infinite`. Restricting to `p.1 < p.2` is an equivalent alternative.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/AmicableNumbers.lean, `type_of% Erdos830.erdos_830.parts.i` imports the unfiltered infinitude statement, including perfect-number diagonals. It therefore asks for infinitely many genuine amicable pairs OR infinitely many perfect numbers, not the Wikipedia question about distinct-member pairs. Unlike the coprime and opposite-parity declarations in this file, this declaration has no condition excluding the diagonal.
findings.source_evidence: The cited https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amicable_numbers says amicable numbers are “two different natural numbers”, asks whether infinitely many pairs exist, and explicitly distinguishes perfect numbers as aliquot sequences of period one. The use-site module's own opening paragraph also specifies distinct positive integers.
findings.suggested_fix: Correct `IsAmicable` or the referenced `Erdos830.erdos_830.parts.i`; the alias will then inherit the corrected statement. Otherwise state infinitude with an explicit distinctness conjunct.

reformulations.difference: The existential variables range over all naturals, with sigma equalities rather than proper-divisor sums, and no explicit positivity hypotheses.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The explicit `a ≠ b` together with `IsAmicable a b` forces both numbers to be positive: if either is zero, its sigma equation forces the other to be zero. Mathlib's identity `σ(n) = sum(properDivisors n) + n` converts the two equations into the usual proper-divisor conditions. I proved the full existential equivalence with distinct positive amicable integers satisfying coprimality.

reformulations.difference: Opposite parity is written `Even a ↔ Odd b`, without explicit distinctness or positivity.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For naturals, this biconditional is equivalent to `(Even a ∧ Odd b) ∨ (Odd a ∧ Even b)`: its false/false case describes odd a and even b. It implies `a ≠ b`, which with the sigma equations implies positivity. I proved the full existential equivalence to the standard distinct-positive amicable-pair question with one even and one odd member.

reformulations.difference: The implemented counting function includes perfect-number diagonals, but this does not change the near-linear lower-bound question.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Write the implemented count as C(x)+P(x), where C counts genuine pairs and P counts perfect numbers. The count decomposition was proved in scratch Lean. The published bound P(x)=O(sqrt(x)), recorded on Wikipedia's Perfect number page with Hornfeck's reference, makes the additional term negligible here. If C+P > x^(1-o(x)), eventually P ≤ (1/2)x^(1-o(x)), hence C > (1/2)x^(1-o(x)) = x^(1-o'(x)), with o'(x)=o(x)+log(2)/log(x) tending to zero. The converse follows from C ≤ C+P. The analytic equivalence was not formalized in Lean.

reformulations.difference: The zero-density statement uses a count that includes perfect-number diagonals.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: With the same decomposition A=C+P, the known bound P(x)=O(sqrt(x)) gives P=o(x). Therefore A=o(x) if and only if C=o(x), by adding or subtracting P. Thus the counting definition has a genuine semantic defect, but it does not change this particular density statement. Only the finite counting decomposition, not this analytic equivalence, was proved in the scratch file.

module

public import Mathlib.NumberTheory.ArithmeticFunction.Misc

@[expose] public section

/-!
# Amicable numbers

Two distinct positive integers $a$ and $b$ are amicable if $\sigma(a) = \sigma(b) = a + b$,
where $\sigma$ is the sum-of-divisors function.
-/

open scoped ArithmeticFunction.sigma

/--
We say that $a,b\in \mathbb{N}$ are an amicable pair if $a \ne b$ and
$\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$. These conditions imply that both numbers are positive.
-/
@[mk_iff]
structure IsAmicable (a b : ℕ) : Prop where
  left : σ 1 a = a + b
  right : σ 1 b = a + b
  ne : a ≠ b
